Abstract
Linear activation steering is a powerful approach for eliciting the capabilities of large language models
and specializing their behavior using limited labeled data. While effective, existing methods often apply
a fixed steering strength to all tokens, resulting in inconsistent steering quality across diverse input
prompts.
In this work, we introduce Contextual Linear Activation Steering (CLAS), a method that
dynamically adapts linear activation steering to context-dependent steering strengths.
Across eleven
steering benchmarks and four model families, it consistently outperforms standard linear activation
steering and matches or exceeds the performance of ReFT and LoRA in settings with limited labeled
data. We therefore propose CLAS as a scalable, interpretable, and accurate method for specializing and
steering large language models.1

Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) [9, 39] exhibit powerful capabilities, yet the underlying mechanisms that give
rise to these capabilities remain largely opaque. A promising lens for mechanistic understanding is provided
by the linear representation hypothesis [19, 24–28], a key empirical observation positing that semantic con-
cepts in LLMs, which form the basis of their capabilities, are represented as fixed linear directions within
their activation spaces. A common approach for identifying such concepts is probing [2, 3, 7, 8, 17, 33],
wherein a dataset of prompts and concept labels is used to train a model on the internal activations of an
LLM to measure the amount of concept-specific information encoded in those activations. Beyond their use
in concept detection, linear directions extracted from these probes can also enable linear activation steering
(LAS) [5, 6, 21, 34, 40], where model generations are steered toward concept-specific behavior by adding
these directions back into the activations during inference. In particular, let hℓ,t ∈Rk denote the activation
at the output of the ℓ-th transformer block2 and the t-th token position of an LLM, and let dℓ∈Rk be a
unit-norm steering vector extracted from a probe trained on the output of block ℓ. LAS involves replacing
hℓ,t during inference with ˜hℓ,t = hℓ,t + αdℓ, where α ∈R is a scalar steering coefficient. This simple yet
general approach has been used to induce and control numerous latent capabilities in LLMs such as sentiment
control [34], reasoning [4], and persona adoption [6], among many others [5].
While LAS is remarkably simple and effective, selecting steering coefficients that perform well across diverse
prompts remains a key bottleneck in practice [5]. This is because the steering coefficient α is often tuned
via an expensive grid search over coefficient values, requiring human or LLM evaluations of the generated
outputs to select the best value [6, 11, 13, 20, 21, 30, 34, 35, 40]. Importantly, a more fundamental limitation
is that these coefficients are context-independent: a fixed scalar is applied uniformly to all inputs, ignoring
variations in prompt or context, and frequently to all blocks of the model [5, 6]. This limitation leads to
systematic under- or over-steering, making current approaches brittle with respect to the choice of α and
limiting real-world deployment, where α cannot be tuned per-prompt or on-the-fly.

To address these limitations, we introduce Contextual Linear Activation Steering (CLAS), which modulates
the amount of steering based on the input context and the specific model block using a learned sensing vector
cℓ∈Rk+1. This sensing vector enables context-dependent activation steering: ˜hℓ,t = hℓ,t + (cℓ· [hℓ,t 1])dℓ,
where [hℓ,t 1] ∈Rk+1 is the concatenation of hℓ,t ∈Rk with a constant 1, and dℓ∈Rk is an extracted
steering vector. To learn the sensing vector, we minimize the standard next-token prediction objective on a
small dataset of prompt-completion pairs. This differs from tuning the coefficients in LAS, which uses an
evaluator to select a fixed coefficient that produces the best generated outputs over a set of prompts.
We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on 11 diverse steering tasks using four instruction-tuned LLMs.
In these tasks, the LLMs are steered to execute behaviors such as step-by-step reasoning, multilingual
translation, tldr-style summarization, and other behaviors without explicit instruction and with only limited
completion data for tuning. We compare our method against LAS and two popular parameter-efficient fine-
tuning baselines, ReFT [37] and LoRA [18]. We find that our method outperforms LAS in nearly every
model-task pair and is significantly faster to tune. We also find that CLAS matches or exceeds both ReFT
and LoRA in these settings. We additionally evaluate whether the low-rank directions learned by ReFT and
LoRA encode interpretable concepts by testing them as linear probes on 11 concept monitoring tasks. We
find that they can be used for concept monitoring, but the probe-derived steering vectors used by CLAS
consistently achieve much higher accuracy. Together, these results demonstrate that CLAS is a scalable and
general extension of linear activation steering, retaining its interpretability while achieving high performance
across many tasks.
Paper outline. In Section 2, we introduce our context-dependent activation steering method, CLAS, and
describe its implementation for steering, including how to obtain the per-block steering and sensing vectors.
In Section 3, we give an overview of the 11 steering tasks and their associated datasets, define the baselines,
describe the experimental setup, and specify how we evaluate steering performance. In Section 4, we present
results on the 11 steering tasks, which include steering and evaluating each task separately, as well as
measuring how steering toward a single task interferes with performance on the other tasks. In Section 5,
we evaluate how the probe-derived steering vectors used by CLAS and the low-rank directions learned by
ReFT and LoRA perform on 11 concept monitoring tasks. In Section 6, we conclude with a brief summary.

3.2
Experimental setup and baselines
We compare CLAS to LAS, LoRA, and ReFT on all 11 steering tasks. CLAS and LAS are activation steering
methods, while LoRA and ReFT are fine-tuning methods. For each task, activation steering methods use
the probe dataset for steering vector extraction and the steer dataset for coefficient tuning. Fine-tuning
methods use only the steer dataset to update a subset of the model parameters.
Baselines. LAS is a context-independent activation steering method: ˜h = h + αd. The steering vector d
can be obtained in many ways [5]. Here, it is obtained from an RFM probe following [6]. LoRA [18] is a
fine-tuning method that adds trainable rank-r matrices A ∈Rr×q and B ∈Rk×r to the frozen model weights
W ∈Rk×q of any MLP layer: ˜h = W x + BAx. ReFT [37] is a fine-tuning method that adds trainable
rank-r matrices to the activations of any layer. Here we consider its DiReFT variation, which adds matrices
W1, W2 ∈Rr×k and bias b ∈Rr to the activations: ˜h = h + W T
2 (W1h + b).
Setup. CLAS, LAS, and ReFT are applied to the residual stream activations after each LLM transformer
block, while LoRA is applied to the final MLP weight W that outputs into the residual stream. For each
task, LAS and CLAS use identical steering vectors {dℓ}L
ℓ=1, extracted from RFM probes trained on the
corresponding probe dataset using the same process as described in Section 2.1. For LAS, α is selected via
grid search to maximize the o3-mini or exact match accuracy used during evaluation on prompts in the steer
dataset. For CLAS, the sensing vectors {cℓ}L
ℓ=1 are learned by minimizing the next-token prediction loss
on the prompt-completion pairs in the steer dataset. ReFT and LoRA use this same objective and dataset
for fine-tuning. All methods use parameter-matched rank-1 adapters, with placement and rank fixed rather
than tuned per method, model, or task. Exact hyperparameters for all methods are provided in Appendix F.

Concept monitoring
Here, we evaluate CLAS, LoRA, and ReFT on 11 concept monitoring tasks. In concept monitoring, we
pass a prompt through an LLM to detect what concept or task is present in its activations. We do this by
projecting the last-token prompt activation hℓ,T from a given block onto a probe direction dℓto obtain a
scalar feature aℓ= (hℓ,T · dℓ). This is done at every block, and a separate linear regression model is trained
on {a(i)
ℓ}N
i=1 at each block to detect concept presence on a set of prompts.
ReFT and LoRA learn low-rank matrices during fine-tuning. In the rank-1 setting, these matrices reduce to
vectors (W T
2 for ReFT and B for LoRA, as defined in Section 3.2), which define directions that can be used
for linear probing. In contrast, CLAS uses a steering vector at each block which is the RFM probe direction,
corresponding to the principal eigenvector of the AGOP (Section 2.1). High linear probe accuracy indicates

Conclusion
Linear activation steering is a powerful approach for eliciting the capabilities of large language models. Yet
despite its success, current steering methods often rely on fixed steering coefficients that do not adapt to
context and that are computationally expensive to tune, limiting their reliability, precision, and scalability.
In this work, we address this limitation with CLAS, which makes the steering coefficient context-dependent.
Our results demonstrate that CLAS outperforms steering with a fixed coefficient and matches or exceeds
fine-tuning methods such as ReFT and LoRA in limited labeled data settings.
Importantly, it does so
while preserving the interpretability of the activation probe directions, enabling accurate concept monitoring
while making the directions more effective for steering.
More broadly, these findings demonstrate that
existing steering directions can become substantially more effective when modulated with context-dependent
coefficients, enabling more precise, scalable, and general control of LLM behavior.

Probe vs. fine-tuning steering direction similarity
We compute similarities between the per-block steering directions used by CLAS, LoRA, and ReFT for
steering. In CLAS, the direction at each transformer block is the RFM probe direction. In LoRA and ReFT,
the direction at each block is learned during fine-tuning to steer model outputs toward target completions.
The per-block steering direction is the MLP weight matrix B for LoRA and W T
2 for ReFT (see Section 3.2
for details). For each block, we compute the unsigned cosine similarity between the directions of two different
methods. Table 16 reports the mean and standard deviation of these similarities aggregated over all blocks.
LoRA and ReFT directions show partial task-dependent alignment due to their shared fine-tuning objective,
while RFM directions remain comparatively orthogonal to them on average. All directions are taken from
early stopping checkpoints, though we observe that LoRA and ReFT directions become even more aligned
at the final checkpoints. Nevertheless, all methods produce similar prompted behaviors on most tasks.

Hyperparameters
The following hyperparmaters are used for the experiments conducted in Section 4–5.
Hyperparameters for steering vector extraction
For each task, we pass the probe dataset prompts through an LLM, train an RFM probe at each transformer
block to predict the corresponding concept label, and extract a steering vector from each probe.
The
RFM hyperparameter search space is the same for all tasks and transformer blocks: L (kernel bandwidth)
∈{1, 1.5, 10, 100}, λ (regularization parameter) ∈{10−3, 10−2, 10−1}, t (number of AGOP iterations) ∈
(0, 10]. We select the best hyperparameter combination via grid search that maximizes the unsigned Pearson
correlation between the last-token prompt residual stream activations projected onto the principal AGOP
eigenvector and the concept labels on a validation set. For each block, the principal AGOP eigenvector
associated with the best hyperparameter setting is used as the per-block steering vector.
Hyperparameters for coefficient tuning and fine-tuning
For each task, we use the prompt-completion pairs from the steer dataset for coefficient tuning and fine-tuning.
For LAS, we tuned the steering coefficient α by generating a completion for each prompt in the steer dataset,
using batch size 1 and limited to 1024 new tokens per prompt. Each completion is evaluated with o3-mini
or exact match (see ”Steering Evaluation” for each task in Section G). We sweep over the same 20 uniformly
spaced coefficients ([0.2, 4] for Qwen, [0.05, 1] for Llama) for each task and select the value α that maximizes
evaluator accuracy. All selected coefficients lie within the ranges defined for each model family, which differ
due to activation norms.
LAS is tuned exclusively using evaluator feedback and does not use the steer
dataset completions.
For CLAS, ReFT, and LoRA, we minimize the standard next-token prediction loss on the steer dataset so
that, given a prompt, the model is steered to produce the desired completion. This is done using AdamW
with learning rate 3 × 10−3 and effective batch size 10 (batch size 1 with 10 gradient accumulation steps),
for up to 8 update steps, with early stopping based on validation loss (not evaluator accuracy). The number
of training and validation samples is identical for each steer dataset, and the same hyperparameters are used
across all methods, models, and tasks. The only exception is the coefficient bias learning rate for CLAS,
which is set to 5 × 10−1 for Qwen and 1 × 10−1 for Llama models.
Hyperparameters for concept monitoring
For each task, we pass the probe dataset prompts through an LLM and, at each transformer block, project
the last-token prompt activations onto a unit-norm steering direction and train a linear regression model
on the resulting projections to predict the concept label. The linear model is tuned over the regularization
strengths λ ∈{10−4, 10−3, 10−2, 10−1, 100, 101} to maximize concept detection accuracy on the probe dataset
validation set, with the best linear model selected for test set evaluation.

Dataset prompts and evaluation templates
Each task in Table 1 includes a probe dataset, a steer dataset, and a task-specific steering evaluation template.
Both the probe and steer datasets are derived from an underlying source dataset.
Probe dataset. The probe dataset is used for steering vector extraction and concept monitoring exper-
iments. It is a supervised dataset of prompt-concept label pairs. It is constructed by randomly sampling
prompts from an underlying source dataset and applying two templates to each prompt: a Task Prompt
template that contains task-specific information and a Non-Task Prompt template that does not contain
task-specific information. Prompts using the Task Prompt template are assigned a concept label of y = 1,
and prompts using the Non-Task Prompt template are assigned a concept label of y = 0.
Steer dataset. The steer dataset is used for the steering experiments. It is constructed from the same
underlying source dataset as the probe dataset and uses a corresponding pair of Task and Non-Task Prompt
templates. Non-Task prompts are used for coefficient tuning and fine-tuning. The associated completions are
23


taken from either the underlying source dataset or generated with o3-mini using the Task Prompt, depending
on the task. This is designed to make the model respond to Non-Task prompts as if given Task prompts.
Evaluation. To evaluate steering, we use either o3-mini as a judge or exact match, depending on the task.
For judge-based evaluation, the judge receives the original source dataset prompt, the model completion,
and an evaluation template, and outputs a score normalized to the range [0, 1]. For exact match evaluation,
a python program evaluates the model completion and outputs a score in {0, 1}.

• Alpaca. A steering task designed to induce a model to follow instructions without including the chat

the completions for the steer dataset are taken directly from the source dataset. The corresponding
probe dataset, steer dataset, and steering evaluation template are shown in Figure 3.
